one_liner: Friendly rescue goats trim your lawn, eat weeds, and send playful GoatCam updates plus app-based lawn reports.
target_customers: Suburban homeowner, 38, busy with kids and work: wants low-effort lawn maintenance without chemicals.
Eco-conscious renter or homeowner, 29, small yard or garden: wants a novelty, sustainable alternative to mowing and weeding.
Short-term rental host, 45, manages multiple properties: needs periodic yard upkeep that looks good in listings.

risks: Trust & safety for in-home visits is especially high here because the service brings animals onto private property and requires handling and containment.
Seasonal demand can make a biweekly goat-mowing subscription uneven, especially in holidays or bad weather.
Low willingness to pay is a risk because customers may compare this to cheaper DIY mowing or standard lawn services.

unit_economics.assumptions:
Sector benchmark from home market: typical CAC $30 and churn 8%. Because our price is above the sector average spend of $25/month and the offer includes on-site labor plus live streaming, CAC is assumed higher than benchmark at $45.

Price per month $49 is set just under the emotional $50 threshold while staying above average home spend.

Monthly cost to serve per customer = $34, built line by line:
- People time: $14 for herd wrangling, site setup, grazing supervision, cleanup, and customer support.
- Transport: $8 for fuel, vehicle wear, and moving the herd/equipment.
- Materials: $7 for temporary fencing, water, treats, waste bags, and basic yard protection supplies.
- Insurance: $3 for liability coverage allocation for each active customer.
- Software: $2 for booking, GoatCam hosting, messaging, and report generation.

Why these numbers changed from the market benchmark: we did not change churn because the home-sector benchmark already fits the product category. We raised CAC from $30 to $45 because the service is more expensive than the $25 average home spend and requires trust, scheduling, and in-person delivery. We kept cost to serve at $34 to reflect a thin but realistic service margin for a physical subscription. The result is LTV/CAC 4.17, which sits in the believable 3 to 8 range.

slides: Problem: Lawn care is time-consuming, chemical-heavy, and easy to defer for busy suburban homeowners who want a small yard to look good without mowing, weeding, or spraying. Goatly’s beachhead is a single pilot neighborhood of homeowners with kids and work who want a low-effort, chemical-free result. The execution risk is real: private-property animal visits require trust and safety, plus scheduling and seasonal reliability. So the first question is not whether goats are charming—it’s whether one route can work with repeatable operations and acceptable economics.

Solution: Goatly is a subscription where friendly rescue goats visit a customer’s garden every two weeks to mow grass and eat weeds with zero chemicals. The MVP ships as a tight service loop: route scheduling and booking, an on-site checklist for fence setup, grazing, cleanup, and departure photo, GoatCam live stream during the visit, and a short lawn report in the app. We also include simple customer notifications plus address, yard, pet/safety notes, and pause-service controls.

Market: The lawn care market is a $48B category growing 7.5% annually. Goatly enters through one sharply defined beachhead: one pilot neighborhood of suburban homeowners, with expansion later to eco-conscious renters/homeowners with small yards and short-term rental hosts. The macro tailwinds are real—gig-economy home services, urban apartment gardening, and smart-home sensors—but the first proof point is local route density, not broad category enthusiasm.

Business Model with Unit Economics: Goatly charges $49/month for one biweekly goat visit for a small yard, plus GoatCam access and a short lawn report. The current modeled cost to serve is $34/month: $14 people time, $8 transport, $7 materials, $3 insurance, and $2 software. That implies $15 gross margin per customer per month and 30.6% gross margin. With $45 CAC and 8% monthly churn, modeled LTV is $187.5, LTV/CAC is 4.17, and CAC payback is 3.0 months. Version 3 is about replacing model inputs with pilot measurements: actual cost per visit, route density, service time, CAC by channel, and retention after renewal.

Go-to-Market and 90-Day Plan: Go-to-market for the first 90 days is intentionally narrow: one pilot neighborhood, one primary acquisition channel, one operating playbook. Primary channel: Nextdoor neighborhood posts, supported by local Facebook groups. The 90-day plan is to ship booking, checklist, GoatCam, reports, notifications, and pause-service controls; sign and serve 20 paying customers in that one neighborhood at $49/month; measure actual cost per visit, route density, service time, and before/after lawn outcomes; and track retention through at least one renewal cycle. The Great Goat Takeover stunt is reserved as a local waitlist generator, not the core acquisition engine.

Team Ask: The ask is for help validating the first repeatable neighborhood route. We are not asking investors to believe the assumptions; we are asking them to support the 90-day proof plan that will replace assumptions with verified data. Success means one neighborhood route with 20 paying customers, under-$34 cost to serve in practice, measurable retention after renewal, and an operational trust-and-safety playbook for private-property goat visits.
investor_pitch.closing_line: Goatly makes lawn care chemical-free, memorable, and measurable—one neighborhood route, one primary channel, one biweekly visit at a time.

verdicts.liked: The concept is instantly memorable, visually strong, and the niche is clear enough to test locally. I like the subscription framing, the concrete monthly price, and that you’ve at least attempted unit economics with CAC, churn, margin, and payback. The local, route-based launch plan is sensible for a service business.
verdicts.concern: Show me the numbers. The economics are only as good as the assumptions, and those assumptions look thin for a live-animal, trust-and-safety-heavy operation. $3 insurance and $8 transport feel hand-wavy, and 8% monthly churn for a quirky lawn service may be optimistic. Also, the market is broad at $48B, but your actual initial segment is much smaller, and it’s unclear how defensible this is beyond novelty and local branding.
verdicts.must_fix: Prove the first-route unit economics with a pilot: track real costs per visit, actual churn/retention, and CAC by channel for at least 20 paying customers, then update the model with verified data before pitching scale.

verdicts.liked: This is unforgettable. Goatly has a real category-creating vibe: chemical-free lawn care with rescue goats is vivid, press-worthy, and immediately understandable. The storytelling is strong, the customer use case is clear, and the MVP is sensibly scoped around booking, routing, and service ops.
verdicts.concern: The biggest risk is not demand, it’s execution and economics. Private-property animal service introduces heavy operational, trust-and-safety, zoning, insurance, and seasonal constraints. The unit economics read plausible on paper, but they feel hand-wavy without evidence that routes can stay dense enough and goats can reliably perform across different yard sizes and geographies. Will this change how people live? Maybe—but only if it becomes a repeatable service, not a viral stunt.
verdicts.must_fix: Prove route density with one real pilot: show 10 paying customers on one neighborhood route with actual costs, service time, insurance terms, and before/after lawn outcomes. That would turn this from clever into investable.

verdicts.liked: Clear, memorable wedge with an easy-to-grasp demo effect. The MVP is reasonably defined, and the 90-day plan at least names real operational work: booking, checklist, trust/safety, and a local pilot. I also like that you included unit economics instead of hand-waving.
verdicts.concern: The target customer is still too broad and the business feels more like a stunt than a repeatable service. I’m not convinced a goat-based lawn subscription scales cleanly, and the pitch doesn’t show enough proof that enough customers will pay $49/month versus standard lawn care. The route economics also hinge on assumptions that feel fragile: utilization, insurance, animal handling, and seasonal demand.
verdicts.must_fix: Narrow to one beachhead customer with a concrete pilot geography and one measurable outcome for the first 90 days—for example, 20 suburban homeowners in one neighborhood with a signed pilot price, retention target, and service frequency proof.

verdicts.liked: This is materially better than version 1. You listened: the pitch is now focused on a pilot route, has a concrete 90-day plan, and the unit economics are spelled out with explicit assumptions. I also like that you acknowledged the trust-and-safety and seasonal execution risk instead of pretending it doesn’t exist. Show me the numbers.
verdicts.concern: The numbers are still mostly assumed, not proven. $49/month for biweekly goat visits looks thin once you include real labor, transport, animal handling, insurance, scheduling, and downtime risk; I don’t yet believe the 30.6% margin without pilot data. The market framing is also a bit broad and mixed with unrelated segments, while the beachhead is very small. The moat is unclear beyond a stunt and operational novelty.
verdicts.must_fix: Before raising more money, report verified pilot data for 20 paying customers: actual cost per visit, route density, gross margin, CAC by channel, and 90-day retention, then replace the assumed model with those realized metrics.

verdicts.liked: You fixed the biggest prior gap: this is now anchored to a real neighborhood route, with explicit pilot milestones, unit economics, and a tighter MVP. verdicts.liked: This is materially tighter than last time: you’ve now named one beachhead customer, one pilot geography, a specific 90-day target of 20 paying homeowners, and a clear operating test around route economics, service time, and retention. The MVP is also more concrete, and I like that you’re treating the first phase as proof of a route, not a vague category play. What ships in the first 90 days? You actually answered it.
